section.title: The LORD Will Restore His People
section.sectionRationale: Following the coming King, God turns to His scattered flock. He condemns the false shepherds and worthless idols that left the people leaderless, then promises to raise up true leadership from Judah, the cornerstone and tent peg, and to strengthen, gather, and bring home His people from every land. The good Shepherd will replace the bad ones and restore His flock.
section.thesis: Because idols and false shepherds have left God's people scattered and oppressed, the LORD Himself will visit His flock, raise up true leadership from Judah, and strengthen, redeem, and gather His people home, so that they walk in His name.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the folly of idols and diviners that leave the flock shepherdless; God's anger at the false shepherds and His raising of the cornerstone and true leaders from Judah; and His promise to strengthen, whistle for, redeem, and gather His people from Egypt and Assyria to walk in His name.

verses.text: Ask the LORD for rain in springtime; the LORD makes the storm clouds, and He will give everyone showers of rain and crops in the field.
For idols speak deceit and diviners see illusions; they tell false dreams and offer empty comfort. Therefore the people wander like sheep, oppressed for lack of a {{roeh|shepherd}}.
“My anger burns against the shepherds, and I will punish the leaders. For the LORD of Hosts attends to His flock, the house of Judah; He will make them like His royal steed in battle.
The {{pinnah|cornerstone}} will come from Judah, the {{yated|tent peg}} from him, as well as the battle bow and every ruler together.
They will be like mighty men in battle, trampling the enemy in the mire of the streets. They will fight because the LORD is with them, and they will put the horsemen to shame.

units.label: Gathered and brought home
units.note: redeemed to walk in His name

verses.text: I will strengthen the house of Judah and save the house of Joseph. I will restore them because I have compassion on them, and they will be as though I had not rejected them. For I am the LORD their God, and I will answer them.
Ephraim will be like a mighty man, and their hearts will be glad as with wine. Their children will see it and be joyful; their hearts will rejoice in the LORD.
I will whistle for them to gather, for I have {{padah|redeemed}} them; and they will be as numerous as they once were.
Though I sow them among the nations, they will remember Me in distant lands; they and their children will live and return.
I will bring them back from Egypt and gather them from Assyria. I will bring them to Gilead and Lebanon until no more room is found for them.
They will pass through the sea of distress and strike the waves of the sea; all the depths of the Nile will dry up. The pride of Assyria will be brought down, and the scepter of Egypt will depart.
I will strengthen them in the LORD, and in His name they will walk,” declares the LORD.

roeh.gloss: A shepherd, one who leads, feeds, and protects the flock; in Scripture a standard image for kings and leaders, and for God Himself. The people wander oppressed for lack of a true shepherd, exposed to false leaders and empty idols. The whole passage moves toward the LORD taking up the shepherd's role for His flock, fulfilled in Christ the good Shepherd.

pinnah.gloss: A cornerstone, the foundational stone that anchors and aligns a whole building. Promised to come from Judah, it pictures the stable, God-given leadership that will replace the false shepherds. The image joins the wider biblical theme of the cornerstone, fulfilled in Christ, the sure foundation and chief cornerstone on whom God's people are built.

yated.gloss: A tent peg or the peg driven into a wall to hang weight on. Like the cornerstone, it is an image of firm, dependable support; from Judah will come the peg on which the community's hopes securely hang. Isaiah uses the same image of a peg in a sure place for a faithful leader, pointing beyond human rulers to the reliable One God provides.

padah.gloss: To redeem, to ransom, to secure release by paying a price. God whistles for His scattered people to gather because He has redeemed them; their return rests on His prior act of ransom, not their own effort. It echoes the redemption from Egypt and looks ahead to the greater redemption accomplished by Christ, who ransoms His people from every land and from sin itself.

basic.context: After the coming King, God addresses His scattered flock and the leaders who failed them. The people had turned to idols and diviners for guidance, which gave only empty comfort, so they wandered like sheep without a shepherd. God's anger burns against these false shepherds. He promises to visit His flock and raise up true leadership from Judah, the cornerstone and the tent peg. Then He pledges to strengthen, whistle for, redeem, and gather His people from Egypt, Assyria, and every land, bringing them home to walk in His name.
basic.hermeneutics: This is prophetic promise using pastoral and military imagery. The contrast is between worthless idols and false shepherds on one side and the LORD as true Shepherd on the other. The cornerstone and tent peg from Judah point to God-given leadership fulfilled in the Messiah. The gathering from Egypt and Assyria pictures a new exodus, a homecoming of God's people that reaches beyond the return from exile.
basic.originalLanguages: The flock wanders for lack of a roeh, a shepherd. God promises leadership from Judah, the pinnah, cornerstone, and the yated, tent peg, images of firm support. And He gathers His people because He has padah, redeemed, ransomed them, so their homecoming rests on His prior act of redemption.
basic.typology: The LORD who shepherds His scattered flock points to Christ, the good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. The cornerstone from Judah is fulfilled in Christ, the chief cornerstone. The redeemed people brought home in a new exodus foreshadow the ingathering Christ accomplishes, gathering His scattered children into one.
basic.christ: The empty idols and false shepherds leave the sheep without care, which sets up the promise fulfilled in Jesus. He is the cornerstone from Judah, the sure foundation, and He is the good Shepherd who seeks the lost, heals the broken, and lays down His life for the flock. The redemption on which the homecoming rests is accomplished in His blood, by which He gathers His people from every nation.
basic.god: God is angry at leaders who exploit and mislead His people, and tender toward the flock they neglected. He takes personal responsibility for His sheep, promising to strengthen, redeem, and gather them out of compassion, treating them as though He had never rejected them. He is a redeeming God who brings His people home and enables them to walk in His name.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 34 condemns false shepherds and promises God as Shepherd. John 10 reveals Jesus as the good Shepherd. Psalm 118 and 1 Peter 2 present the cornerstone. Isaiah 11 foretells a second exodus gathering God's people from Assyria and Egypt.
basic.oneStory: God will not leave His flock to idols and false shepherds; He raises the cornerstone from Judah and gathers His redeemed people home in a new exodus. This points to Christ, the good Shepherd and chief cornerstone, who ransoms and gathers His scattered people, and the story runs on toward the one flock brought home to walk forever in His name.

context.literary:
Chapter 10 is a tightly built poem in three panels, and it opens with a small surprise: a command to the people, not a promise to them. 'Ask the LORD for rain,' verse 1, is the first imperative since the call to rejoice in 9:9, and it sets the terms for the whole chapter. The people are to look to the one source of rain, and then the poem shows what happens when they look anywhere else.

The first panel, verses 1 and 2, is a diagnosis. Rain is God's gift, idols and diviners are a lie, and the result of trusting the lie is wandering. The second panel, verses 3 to 5, turns on a pair of words that sound alike in English and are one verb in Hebrew: God will 'punish' the leaders and 'attend to' His flock. A single verb of visitation, with the same root, becomes judgment for the one group and care for the other. The panel ends with the arrival of rulers from Judah, described in four images, a cornerstone, a tent peg, a battle bow and 'every ruler together.' The third panel, verses 6 to 12, is the gathering. God strengthens, saves, restores, whistles, redeems, sows and brings home, and the verbs give the section its pace.

The poem is full of repeated pairs. Judah and Joseph are named in verse 6, then Ephraim in verse 7, so that the two halves of a divided people appear together. Egypt and Assyria are named at the end as the two oppressors of old, and Gilead and Lebanon as the two borders of the restored land. The chapter closes with the first and last of the LORD's strength: 'I will strengthen them in the LORD,' verse 12, which picks up the same verb as in verse 6 and encloses the promise.

The chapter belongs between two others whose emphasis is different. Chapter 9 gave the King, and chapter 11 will show the Shepherd rejected. Chapter 10 is the pastoral middle: what God intends to do for a flock that has had false leaders. Its optimism makes the shock of chapter 11 sharper.
context.historical:
The conditions behind the chapter are those of the early Persian period. Judah was a small province, the northern kingdom had been gone for two centuries, and the old empires, Assyria and Egypt, were either defunct or distant. Yet verse 10 speaks of bringing the people back 'from Egypt' and 'from Assyria.' By Zechariah's day Assyria had fallen to Babylon in the late seventh century BC. Using the name for exiles in lands that Assyria once held is a poetic way of speaking of every place of dispersal, and the book of Ezra can even call the Persian ruler 'the king of Assyria,' Ezra 6:22. Communities of Israelites had indeed settled in Egypt after Jerusalem's fall, Jeremiah 43:5 to 7, and in the old Assyrian lands.

The 'house of Joseph' in verse 6 and 'Ephraim' in verse 7 mean the northern tribes, taken into exile by Assyria in 722 BC. Their reunion with Judah is a repeated hope of the prophets, Ezekiel 37:15 to 22 being the most vivid, with its two sticks becoming one. The promise had real force, since the division between north and south was ancient and bitter.

The charge against idols and diviners reflects temptations that never entirely left. The word the BSB translates 'idols' in verse 2 is, in Hebrew, teraphim, the household images that Rachel took from Laban, Genesis 31:19, and which turn up again in the book of Judges and in Hosea 3:4 as tools for seeking guidance. Diviners were forbidden by the law, Deuteronomy 18:10 to 12. The people who had returned from Babylon were forbidden to consult them, yet the pull of such practices was strong in an anxious age.

The agricultural frame also matters. Spring rain in Israel falls late, in March and April, and decides the grain harvest. A farmer in verse 1 is told to ask for it at the very time he would be worrying about it, and Deuteronomy 11:14 had assigned the autumn and spring rains to God's blessing on a faithful nation.
context.canonical:
The chapter belongs to a family of shepherd passages. Ezekiel 34 is its nearest relative: false shepherds who feed themselves, a scattered flock, God's own search and rescue, and finally one shepherd, David, set over them, Ezekiel 34:23. Jeremiah 23:1 to 4 says the same: shepherds who scatter the sheep will be dealt with, and God will gather the remnant and raise up shepherds who tend them. Zechariah condenses these into two verses and adds the cornerstone from Judah.

The cornerstone image carries its own history. Isaiah 28:16 speaks of a tested stone, a precious cornerstone laid in Zion. Psalm 118:22 says the builders rejected it, and the New Testament reads both together: 1 Peter 2:6 and 7 quotes Isaiah and the Psalm in a single passage, and Paul speaks of Christ Jesus as the cornerstone of the household of God, Ephesians 2:20. Zechariah's cornerstone is a leader who supports the whole structure of a people.

The new exodus pattern is almost continuous. Verses 10 and 11 recall the Red Sea and the plagues of Egypt, and Isaiah 11:15 and 16 does the same in a highway for the remnant from Assyria. Hosea 11:10 and 11 gives the picture of children coming 'like birds from Egypt and like doves from the land of Assyria.' The theme resurfaces in the Gospels, where Jesus' ministry gathers the lost sheep of Israel and John 11:52 speaks of gathering 'the scattered children of God' into one.

The picture of people without a shepherd is repeated in 1 Kings 22:17 and quoted by Jesus in Matthew 9:36 and Mark 6:34, and the Good Shepherd discourse of John 10 draws the contrast between the true Shepherd and the hired hand. In Revelation 7:17 the Lamb in the center of the throne becomes the shepherd of the great multitude, which brings the shepherd theme to its goal.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Zechariah wrote to people who were being tempted to look for guidance and security anywhere except the LORD. The tools were old ones: household images, diviners, dreams, and any leader who would say what they wanted to hear. He answered with a simple contrast. Rain comes from God alone, the other sources speak 'deceit' and 'empty comfort,' and the result of trusting them is a people who drift like sheep with nobody to lead them.

He then wanted the people to hear what God thinks of their leaders. 'My anger burns against the shepherds' is a strong statement, and it should have made the leaders afraid and the flock hopeful. Leaders are accountable to God, and bad leadership is not a tragedy to be shrugged off but an offence that He will deal with. At the same time the people were not to blame everything on their leaders; verse 2 says they wandered because they believed lies, and the shepherd's failure and the flock's credulity went together.

The hope in verses 4 to 12 was meant to be concrete. God would raise leaders from Judah, strengthen both Judah and Joseph, whistle for His people, and bring them back from the old places of captivity. Each verb is something a small and discouraged community could take hold of. The intention was to turn a hopeless population into a people who would act: 'they will remember Me in distant lands,' verse 9.

And the last verse gives the aim in a few words: 'in His name they will walk.' The point of the promise is not only comfort. It is a life of continuous walking, a daily direction, under the LORD.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes God's shepherding and restoring action, and its single clear command is in verse 1: 'Ask the LORD for rain.' That command is permanent. The posture of asking God, in the season when one most feels the pressure of need, belongs to every believer. Jesus' own teaching on asking in Matthew 7:7 to 11 and the word of James 1:5 and 6 continue it.

The condemnation of idols, diviners and false shepherds is partly description and partly warning. It describes what happened to a particular people, but it also shows what happens to any community that looks for security in anything but God. We should be careful not to pick out particular modern practices and call them diviners without seeing the underlying point. The principle is that any voice that promises comfort apart from the truth of God is, in the prophet's terms, an empty comfort.

The military pictures of verses 3 to 5 are not instructions to fight. Judah is called God's 'royal steed in battle,' and its strength is explicitly borrowed, 'because the LORD is with them,' verse 5. A reader should not use them to justify force done in God's name, especially after the previous chapter has said that the weapons of war will be cut off. The application is about dependence.

Finally, the geography of the return, Gilead, Lebanon, Egypt and Assyria, should not be mapped directly onto a modern plan. The text uses these names as the boundary markers of an old story, and the New Testament takes the ingathering and applies it to Christ's gathering of the scattered children of God, John 11:52.

debates.question: Who is the cornerstone from Judah, and the tent peg, and the battle bow?

views.label: Strong leaders arising from Judah in the near future
views.case: The context is a contrast with the false shepherds of verses 2 and 3, and the cluster names the good leadership that God will raise. The passage follows the previous promise of a King and widens it to rulers who share in His strength, 'every ruler together,' who will govern the restored community.

views.label: The Messiah from Judah, described in four images
views.case: Judah is the royal tribe, and 'from him' in each phrase points to one person. The cornerstone, the peg and the bow are three aspects of a single ruler, and the New Testament takes up the same images for Christ: the cornerstone in Ephesians 2:20 and 1 Peter 2:6, and the prince from Judah in Hebrews 7:14.

views.label: Both, in a pattern that culminates in Christ
views.case: The images describe the whole line of Judah's rulers and the community's leadership, and they find their final and decisive meaning in the Messiah, who holds together all God's gifts of leadership.

debates.bearing: On any reading the promise is of God-given, durable leadership from Judah that stands in contrast to the false shepherds, and the New Testament shows Jesus as its fullest form.

debates.question: What does the gathering from Egypt and Assyria promise?

views.label: A literal return of the scattered to the land
views.case: Gilead, Lebanon and the land itself are named, and the promise that 'no more room is found for them' suggests a large return. This view takes the prophets' hope of a restored people in their land as meant.

views.label: A new exodus fulfilled in Christ's gathering
views.case: The sea, the Nile and the pride of Assyria echo the first exodus, and the New Testament speaks of Jesus gathering 'the scattered children of God,' John 11:52. On this view the geography is the language of the old story put to use for a larger rescue.

views.label: Fulfilled in stages, with a final gathering
views.case: Some hold that the return under the Persians began the promise, the gospel carries it on, and a final gathering will complete it, in line with the language of Isaiah 11:11 and 12.

debates.bearing: All three agree that God's redemption precedes and guarantees the homecoming: 'for I have redeemed them,' verse 8.

debates.question: Does the horse imagery of verse 3 contradict 9:10?

views.label: No, the imagery is of God's own strength given to His people
views.case: Judah is a horse of God's choosing, a 'royal steed,' not a horse of Judah's own acquisition, and the point is that God's strength, not human cavalry, will make the people strong. The horse is a metaphor and not an army.

views.label: Yes, it is a tension the book accepts
views.case: Chapter 9 cuts off the horse and chapter 10 uses the horse as a picture of strength, because Hebrew poetry can use the same image for opposite purposes. The book asks the reader to hold both, since military language describes God's victory while the King himself disarms.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is taken, the strength of the people is borrowed from the LORD, and verse 5 states it: they fight 'because the LORD is with them.'

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 asks for rain with a word that carries more than a season. The BSB's 'springtime' rain translates malqosh, the late rain of March and April that fills out the grain before harvest. It is paired in the law with the early rain, yoreh, which falls in autumn and softens the ground for sowing, Deuteronomy 11:14, and in the prophets the two stand together as the promise of a good year, Joel 2:23. Hosea uses the same idea to describe God's coming to His people, 'like the spring showers that water the earth,' Hosea 6:3. A farmer who asks for the late rain is asking for the last, decisive gift of the year.

The 'idols' of verse 2 are teraphim in Hebrew, the household images that Rachel carried away from her father's house, Genesis 31:19. The BSB's rendering is a fair gloss, but the Hebrew word is the more specific and homely one, the object kept in a house to ask questions of. It is joined by qosemim, 'diviners,' from the verb qasam that the law forbids, Deuteronomy 18:10. So the sources of false guidance are not exotic: they are the small, familiar things people keep close.

The verb paqad stands behind both halves of verse 3. God says He will 'punish' the shepherds and 'attend to' His flock, and the BSB renders the same root in two ways because English has no single word for it. The root means to visit, to take notice, and its result depends on whom God visits. It is the verb of Exodus 3:16, where God tells Moses 'I have surely attended to you,' and so the word has a rescue meaning in the story of Israel. The shepherds' judgment and the flock's care are one act of attention seen from two sides.

The footnote to verse 3 offers 'male goats' for what the BSB gives as 'leaders.' The word is attudim, the he-goats that lead a flock, and it is used for leaders in Isaiah 14:9 and for the powerful animals of the flock in Ezekiel 34:17. The picture is of the lead male animals in a herd, who should be the first to guide it and may be the first to bully it. In Ezekiel 34 God judges between sheep and sheep and between rams and goats. Zechariah has taken a term from the animal world to describe human leaders.

The word for 'ruler' in verse 4, nogesh, is also used of those who drive others, the taskmasters of Exodus 3:7 and the oppressor of Zechariah 9:8. Whether it means a ruler or an exactor depends on the context, and here the context is plain: the line that began with a cornerstone ends with every ruler, together, coming out of Judah. A word that had belonged to the overseers of Egypt is now given to the leaders of the restored people.

Verse 6 gives two verbs of compassion. 'I have compassion,' rachamtim, comes from the root racham, which is linked to the word for womb, so that God's mercy is a mother's tenderness. The people will be 'as though I had not rejected them,' from zanach, the verb for casting off. The pairing is effective: the one who cast them off is the one who has a womb-love for them.

In verse 8 'I will whistle' is ashreqah, from sharaq, and it is the shepherd's or beekeeper's call, but also the way God summons nations in Isaiah 5:26. The same sound that calls the scattered sheep calls armies. And in verse 9 'sow' is zara, the verb of planting seed. To scatter among the nations is also to sow, as in Hosea 2:23. In verse 12 the verb 'walk' is a reflexive form, hithallek, which describes continual, habitual walking and is used of Enoch, who 'walked with God,' Genesis 5:24.

typology.fulfillment: The cornerstone holds a building together and sets its lines, and Zechariah says it will come from Judah. Isaiah had laid a 'tested stone' in Zion, Isaiah 28:16, and the Psalm says the builders rejected it, Psalm 118:22. In the New Testament Christ Jesus is 'the cornerstone' of a building made of believers, Ephesians 2:20, and Peter says the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone, 1 Peter 2:7. The type is limited in that Zechariah's stone supports a nation's leadership; the stone in Christ supports a temple of living people drawn from every nation.

typology.type: The LORD attending His flock, verses 3 and 8
typology.fulfillment: God's promise to visit His flock and to whistle them home takes shape in Jesus the Shepherd. He saw the crowds as sheep without a shepherd, Matthew 9:36, and said 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11. Peter says believers who were like sheep going astray have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls, 1 Peter 2:25. The escalation is the cost: Zechariah's shepherd gathers with a whistle, and Jesus gathers with His own life, which is the redemption of verse 8 made concrete.

typology.type: The crossing of the sea of distress, verse 11
typology.fulfillment: The people will pass through the sea and the depths of the Nile will dry up, recalling the Red Sea, Exodus 14:21 and 22. Isaiah had already described a second drying of the waters for the remnant, Isaiah 11:15 and 16. The pattern is fulfilled in the work of Christ, whom Matthew presents as the new Israel called out of Egypt, Matthew 2:15, and whose death and resurrection Paul compares to passing through the sea, 1 Corinthians 10:1 and 2. The correspondence is of exodus and deliverance; it fails to match in that the first crossing freed a nation from a tyrant, and the final one frees the world from sin and death.

typology.type: Judah and Joseph restored as one flock, verses 6 and 7
typology.fulfillment: The two houses of Judah and Joseph, divided for centuries, are brought together, as in the vision of the two sticks in Ezekiel 37:15 to 22, where one king rules them all. In Jesus the promise of one flock under one shepherd is stated plainly, 'there will be one flock and one shepherd,' John 10:16, and Paul says He made the two groups one, tearing down the dividing wall, Ephesians 2:14. The type points beyond the reunion of two tribes to the union of Jew and Gentile, and it is not yet complete while divisions remain in the church.

study.christ:
The chapter points to Christ first through the emptiness it describes. A flock 'oppressed for lack of a shepherd,' verse 2, is a condition the Gospels return to. When Jesus looked at the crowds He had compassion on them 'because they were like sheep without a shepherd,' Mark 6:34, and Matthew says they were 'harassed and helpless,' Matthew 9:36. His response in both cases is to act as the Shepherd: He teaches them, feeds them, heals them. What Zechariah had said God would do, Jesus does in front of the people, and the Gospels invite us to see the connection.

The chapter also points to Christ through the cornerstone. When the prophet speaks of the cornerstone coming 'from Judah,' he places the leader in the royal tribe that Genesis 49:10 had promised the scepter. Hebrews says plainly that 'our Lord descended from Judah,' Hebrews 7:14, and Matthew's genealogy runs through Judah to David and to Jesus, Matthew 1:2 to 6. The apostles then use the stone images of Isaiah and the Psalms for Him. Peter quotes Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:22 together in 1 Peter 2:6 and 7, and Paul says Christ Jesus Himself is the cornerstone of the household of God, Ephesians 2:20. Elsewhere Paul says that no one can lay another foundation than the one already laid, 1 Corinthians 3:11. A reader of Zechariah 10:4 who knows the rest of the Bible hears in 'the cornerstone will come from Judah' a promise that God's people will be held together by one person.

The tent peg adds something. A peg holds a tent to the ground and carries the weight of whatever is hung on it. Isaiah 22:23 to 25 uses the image of a peg driven into a firm place on which the whole household's weight hangs, and it also warns that a human peg can give way. In Christ the peg does not give way, since He bears the whole weight of His people's sins and hopes, 1 Peter 2:24. That is an application of the image, not a claim that Zechariah had it in mind, and it should be held lightly.

The promise of redemption in verse 8 points to the cross. God says He will whistle for His people because He has redeemed them, and the Gospels say the Son of Man came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. The redemption is the basis of the homecoming, and the New Testament names the price: believers were purchased by Christ's blood, Acts 20:28 and Revelation 5:9.

And the gathering from far countries leads to Christ in the words of John 11:52, where the evangelist says Jesus would die 'not only for the nation, but also for the scattered children of God, to gather them together into one.' Jesus Himself declares, 'I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them in as well,' John 10:16. The great Shepherd is the one who gathers, and the end of the story is the Lamb who becomes their shepherd, Revelation 7:17.

We should not make every detail of the chapter into a code for Jesus. The rain, the goats and the horse are not secret references. The connection is with the shepherd's task, the leader from Judah and the redemption that precedes the gathering.
study.god:
The chapter's first claim about God is that He alone gives what the land and the people need. Verse 1 says 'the LORD makes the storm clouds' and 'will give everyone showers of rain,' so the idols that speak deceit are not merely wrong but powerless. God is Lord of the weather and the harvest, which is why Jeremiah asks, 'Can the worthless idols of the nations bring rain?' Jeremiah 14:22. The doctrine of God that follows is that everything good the creature receives comes by His hand.

He is a God who judges leaders. 'My anger burns against the shepherds' is not a general complaint. It is an anger that arises from His love for the flock. Leaders hold their office on trust, and the God who appoints them watches how they use it. It is one of the most consoling thoughts in the passage for people who have suffered under bad leadership, and one of the most sobering for those who lead.

He attends to His own. The same verb that punishes the shepherds gives care to the flock, and the chapter says He will 'make them like His royal steed in battle,' verse 3. A herd of small, anxious sheep becomes a war horse in His hands. God does not simply rescue the weak; He dignifies them and makes them strong, and He does it by being with them, 'because the LORD is with them,' verse 5.

He is compassionate beyond what the people deserve. 'I have compassion on them, and they will be as though I had not rejected them,' verse 6. The rejection was real, the exile was a real casting off, and yet the compassion removes it, as if it had not happened. This holds together two things that seem to pull apart, the justice that sent them away and the love that brings them back. God is not forced by one into betraying the other; He is both.

He is a God who answers: 'I am the LORD their God, and I will answer them,' verse 6. The prayer of verse 1 is promised an answer in verse 6. This ties the whole chapter into a pattern of asking and answering.

He redeems before He gathers. 'I will whistle for them to gather, for I have redeemed them,' verse 8. The call is rooted in a deed already done, and the people hear the whistle as those who have been bought. And He does not forget those who have gone far. 'They will remember Me in distant lands,' verse 9, is God's promise to keep a memory alive in them, a sign of His patient work in the hearts of exiles.

For worship the chapter asks for two responses. The first is to ask, as verse 1 commands, with confidence that the One we ask is the Giver of every good gift. The second is to walk, as verse 12 says, in His name, which means living under His authority and character in the ordinary movement of days. Strength is to be found 'in the LORD,' and nowhere else.

crossReferences.note: The law ties the autumn and spring rains to love and obedience, 'then I will provide rain for your land in season.' Zechariah 10:1 takes up the promise and turns it into an instruction: since rain comes from the LORD, ask Him for it. It shows that the chapter's opening command rests on a promise already given.

A prayer in a drought: 'Can the worthless idols of the nations bring rain?' The answer is no, and the people hope in the LORD. Zechariah 10:2 pushes the same argument, that idols and diviners offer nothing, and shows that the people were still tempted by the same false confidence.

God Himself promises to search for His flock, bring them out from the peoples, feed them and bind up the broken. Zechariah 10 is a short version of the same promise, with the same movement from false shepherds to the LORD's own care. The Ezekiel text supplies the detail that Zechariah assumes.

Two sticks, Judah and Joseph, are joined into one in the prophet's hand, and one king rules over the reunited people. This is the same hope as Zechariah 10:6 and 7, where Judah and Joseph are strengthened together. It shows the long expectation of healing the old split between north and south.

God lays in Zion 'a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation,' and whoever believes will not be shaken. It is the background of the cornerstone in Zechariah 10:4. Both texts connect the stone with security for the people, and the New Testament connects both with Christ.

A highway for the remnant from Assyria, as there was for Israel when they came out of Egypt, with the waters dried for crossing. This is the closest parallel to Zechariah 10:10 and 11, where the same two lands and the same drying of waters mark the new exodus. The two prophets share a vocabulary of deliverance.

The LORD roars like a lion and His children come trembling 'like birds from Egypt and like doves from the land of Assyria.' Egypt and Assyria again stand for the lands of exile, and the return is accompanied by God's voice. The echo with Zechariah's whistle suggests that God calls His people in a voice they cannot ignore.

Jesus sees the crowds as 'harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.' The scene recalls Zechariah 10:2 and shows Jesus identifying Himself as the Shepherd that the people lack. It is one of the clearest places where the Gospel writer makes the Old Testament shepherd theme a description of Jesus' ministry.

Jesus says He is the good shepherd who lays down His life, contrasts Himself with the hired hand who runs from the wolf, and promises one flock and one shepherd. It carries Zechariah 10 forward, with the gathering from beyond the fold, the sheep who know His voice and the cost of the shepherd's care.

Caiaphas unknowingly prophesies that Jesus would die for the nation and for the scattered children of God, 'to gather them together into one.' The word 'scattered' and the aim of gathering link directly to Zechariah's promise of the dispersed being brought home.

Peter joins Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:22 and applies them to Jesus: a chosen and precious cornerstone to those who believe, and a stone rejected by the builders. This is how the church read the cornerstone images of the Old Testament, and it gives Zechariah 10:4 its Christian setting.

The Lamb in the center of the throne becomes the shepherd of the great multitude and leads them to springs of living water. It is the final fulfilment of the shepherd promises. The flock Zechariah saw wandering without a shepherd finds the Shepherd and is led to water.

study.oneStory:
The chapter picks up the problem that has run through the Bible since Genesis 3: a people made to be led by God keep turning to other voices. The serpent was the first diviner, a voice that spoke deceit and offered empty comfort, and every idol after him has the same shape. By Zechariah's day the pattern had cost Israel its land, its king and its temple, and the lesson was meant to be learned: only God gives rain, only God shepherds.

It also takes up the story of the shepherds. Moses and David were shepherds before they were leaders, and the word for the king's task in the Old Testament is the word for pastoring a flock. When Israel's rulers failed, God Himself took up the staff, as Ezekiel 34 and Jeremiah 23 say. Zechariah 10 stands at a point where the promise of a faithful shepherd is renewed but not yet fulfilled, and the people are left looking for the one who will be both the LORD and a man from Judah.

The chapter's end rehearses the exodus once more. Israel's founding event was a crossing of the sea out of Egypt, and the prophets insisted that God would do it again. Isaiah 11, Jeremiah 16:14 and 15, Hosea 11 and Zechariah 10 all say that a second exodus is coming, bigger than the first. The return from Babylon was a first fulfilment, but the language outran it.

What follows in the story is both promise and shock. In chapter 11 the Shepherd is rejected and the flock is handed over to worse shepherds, and in chapter 13 the Shepherd is struck and the sheep scattered. The great hope of chapter 10 passes through this darkness, and the Gospels tell the same story. Jesus gathers the lost sheep, is struck, and the flock scatters, Mark 14:27, and then He rises and gathers them again, so that 'there will be one flock and one shepherd,' John 10:16.

The new creation is where the chapter lands. The Lamb is the shepherd, and the people of every nation are brought home, no longer scattered or oppressed, led to springs of living water, Revelation 7:17. The cornerstone has become the foundation of a city whose foundations carry the names of the apostles, Revelation 21:14. The God who made rain and storm clouds dwells with His people, and nothing in all creation is left to false shepherds.

quiz.q: Why do the people wander like sheep?

options.text: They lack a true shepherd and have turned to idols and diviners for empty comfort.
options.note: Verse 2, oppressed for lack of a shepherd, misled by idols and false dreams.

options.text: They have too many good shepherds to follow.
options.note: The problem is the absence of a true shepherd, not too many.

options.text: They refused all rain and food from God.
options.note: Verse 1 invites them to ask God for rain; the core issue is false guidance.

options.text: For no reason the passage gives.
options.note: The text names idols and lack of a shepherd as the reason.

quiz.q: What does God promise will come from Judah?

options.text: The cornerstone, the tent peg, and true leadership for the flock.
options.note: Verse 4 names the cornerstone and tent peg from Judah.

options.text: More idols and diviners.
options.note: God replaces idols with firm, true leadership, not more idols.

options.text: A foreign king to rule them.
options.note: The leadership comes from Judah, not from foreign powers.

options.text: Nothing at all.
options.note: God promises the cornerstone and true leaders from Judah.

quiz.q: On what basis does God gather His scattered people?

options.text: Because He has redeemed them, having ransomed them Himself.
options.note: Verse 8, I will whistle for them to gather, for I have redeemed them.

options.text: Because they earned their return by good works.
options.note: The gathering rests on God's redemption, not their merit.

options.text: Because the nations released them freely.
options.note: God redeems and gathers them; the nations do not free them.

options.text: He does not gather them.
options.note: He gathers them from Egypt, Assyria, and every land.

quiz.q: How is the cornerstone from Judah fulfilled?

options.text: In Christ, the chief cornerstone and sure foundation of God's people.
options.note: 1 Peter 2 and Psalm 118 present Christ as the cornerstone.

options.text: In a literal stone kept in the temple.
options.note: The cornerstone points to a person, ultimately Christ.

options.text: In the false shepherds God condemns.
options.note: The cornerstone replaces the false shepherds, fulfilled in Christ.

options.text: It is never fulfilled.
options.note: It is fulfilled in Christ the chief cornerstone.

quiz.q: What does God intend for His restored people beyond bringing them home?

options.text: To strengthen them in the LORD so they walk in His name.
options.note: Verse 12, I will strengthen them, and in His name they will walk.

options.text: To leave them to fend for themselves.
options.note: He strengthens them rather than abandoning them.

options.text: To scatter them again immediately.
options.note: He gathers and strengthens them, not scatters them.

options.text: Nothing beyond a change of location.
options.note: He aims for a changed life walking in His name, not just relocation.

questions: The people sought guidance from idols that gave empty comfort. Where do you turn for direction that cannot really help, instead of asking the LORD?
God's anger burns against shepherds who exploit the flock. How does this shape the way you pray for and choose the leaders you follow?
Christ is the good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. How does it comfort you to be cared for by Him rather than by failed leaders?
God gathers His people because He has redeemed them, not because they earned it. How does resting in His redemption change the way you approach Him?
God's goal is that His people walk in His name. What would it look like this week to walk in the LORD's name in your ordinary life?

translationNotes.note: Leaders can be rendered literally male goats, a figure for the ruling shepherds against whom God's anger burns before He attends to His flock.
Cornerstone, tent peg, and battle bow are images of firm support and strength emerging from Judah; Isaiah 22:23 uses the peg in a sure place for a faithful leader, pointing beyond human rulers.
Passing through the sea of distress and drying up the Nile evokes a new exodus, picturing God's gathering of His redeemed people home from every land.
